title: Favorite tunes and spirituals
summary: He likes both pop standards and old spirituals such as Closer Walk and Ole Miss, which Oliver played at Tulane Gym.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days

blocks.x: Oh, one other question I was going to ask about different tunes. Do you have any idea on should you be able to play any kind of a pop commercial Tin Pan Alley tune? Or do you like some of the old Dixieland favorites? Are there blues? Or what kind of numbers are best for a jazz band? Or what do you enjoy playing? Or what do you think they should play?

Oh, well, I think some numbers out of each category. Are good. Numbers, of course, like rumbas and things like that are kind of hard to do much with. But ordinarily, well, the pieces that have stuck, like My Blue Heaven and Out of the Popular Group, are always good. And Indiana, my home in Indiana, those stick all the time. I mean, you can't get rid of them. And those are popular. Of course, most of the jazz tunes lend themselves to jazz naturally.
The pieces that I love most of all are the old Negro sort of spirituals. You know, like, in so long since I've played, I can't even think of the name. Yeah.
What is it? Just Closer Walk.
Closer Walk with E. And Pattern on the Floor.

Somewhere around the hill. Yeah. Yeah. And Old Miss. Old Miss. Yeah. I love that tune. The way Joe Oliver used to play it up in Tulane Gym. He just played the chorus. He didn't play the whole arrangement, which, by the way, is terrific. The whole arrangement is fine.
It was always in Bugle Call Rag. They used it as a special, like, trio section.
Well, I, you know, you know who Face put it on a record? I did with Tony Perranti. We played, we got a tune which was a blues.
Ole Miss into it. In the dungeon. That was the first time.
